summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,23,994/ as the net wealth of the assessee on the outstandings of the money lending business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed the view taken by the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments and that the High Court erred in holding that accrued interests were liable to he included in wealth tax assessment. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net assets of an assessee call for a determination of his assets and debts as on the valuation date. [310C] 2. The scheme of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, the net value of an asset which is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the wealth Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the Valuation date. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be excluded within the assets of the asses see under the Wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assesses are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, although not realised, on the Outstandings, of the moneys lending business are liable to been included in its net wealth. [309F G] 3. The principle of apportionment of the assets amongst the assessee has been recognised by the statute and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by the assessee. [311G H] 4. The concept of "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value" of all the assets belonging to the assessee, on valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate value of all those debts owed by the assesseee on the date of valuation. All the assets, of a assessee, bar those expressly excepted by the Statute, are to be taken into account and it was immaterial whether such income employs one method of accounting adopted by him. [312A B] 5. The principles of apportionment laid down in the last day of the income tax "previous year" do not apply to the assets which are specifically excluded by the statutes. [313C D] 6. The provisions of section 7(1) and (2) of the Act have been made applicable to the wealth of an assesses under the Income tax Act, and that being so there is no reason why the principle of distribution of the value of the asset amongst the assesees on the basis of the out standings of money lending. [317D] 7. The expression "net assets" which speak of "in the excess of what is actually adopted" in the statute means only those assets which have been included within the net Wealth of the assessees and not those which are excluded by any other consideration of a statute. [320F G; 321A] 8.

The respondent was a workman in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed misconduct and was not found guilty of any misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for setting aside the order of dismissal. The Tribunal held that the punishment of dismissal should be maintained but set aside the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority. The appellant company preferred a writ petition in this Court challenging the order passed by the Tribu nal on the grounds that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal was based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has no juris diction under Article 226 of the Constitution to interfere in a case where the Tribunal is satisfied that if some but not all of t he findings of the Tribunal were "unreasonable", the order cannot be sustained. [27F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal imposed a lesser penalty on the respond ent. The Court has not gone into the question whether the punishment imposed by th e disciplinary authority can be supported on any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority in imposing the punishment. [28F] 3.2 The Tribunal has no jurisdiction if the findings of t his Inquiry Officer are based on the evidence even though some of them may be found to he irrelevant or irrelevant. If the inference that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the appellant was too seve rred, it was not for thority to consider any finding on substantial misdemeanor for which t he punishment could lawfully be impose, it has no merits. [29F] 4. The order of the Tribun al imposing a lesser punishment on the appel lant cannot, therefore, be sustained.[30A B] 5. In Shankar Dass vs Union of India this Court set aside t he impugned order of penalty on t he ground that the imposition of the penalty was too harsh to the responde nt. [31F G] 6. The question whether a punishment of dismissing from service passed by an authority can he supported on some finding as regards substantial misdemeano f for which no penalty can lawfully been imposed, is not deter mined in this case since the respondent had already retired from service and his reinstatement in service was not challenged. [32F G; 33A] 7. The res pondent has failed to establish any misconduct or negligence on his part. If it is his case that he was not in fact the person convicted, it would be open to him to challenge the finding of the inquiry officer or the Tribuna nal. [33G H] 8. In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of the aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the tribunal imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot, however, be justified. [34F G].

The first ground on which the High Court dismissed the suit was that the suit for a declaration and injunction was barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968 filed by the appellants. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners are carpenters in the Government service. They have been working as daily rated employees. Their services were terminated by the Corporation on the ground that they had not completed 240 days of work in a year. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the termination of their services. This Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners are not entitled to any relief. In the appeal, it was contended for the Corporation that the unit where the petition ers were working is a factory registered under the Factories Act and the Government has not fixed the mini mum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. There is no discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment. [667B] 2. The Corporation has no regularly employed carpenter nor it is a mere recent decision which has exhaustively dealt with all the principles bearing on the question of equal pay for Equal work in that principle. [668C D] 3. The Court held that the principle of 'equal pay ' for equal works cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It is not permissible to provide two different pay scales in the similar cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [669D] 4. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected. [670E F] 5. The court held that it is open to the State to classify employees on the same basis as the selection based upon merit with proper regard to competence and efficiency. [671F] 6. The principles of " equal pay" for equal Work cannot be enforced in every type of service especially in the areas of professional service. It has not been extended to employees of the Corporation. The petitioners have been treated as construction workers and they are being paid the minimum wages admissible to such workmen. [672F] 7. The writ petitions fail and are dismissed.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Judge, Mehsana, in respect of murder of Malan and acquitted them. The High Court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against accused 1 to 4 beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted all the accused except accused 5. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of PW 2, who had been tried along with accused 1, 6 and 7 was under section 34 read with Section 120B I. P.C., and that the conviction could not be sustained because they were acquitted by the High Court; (ii) the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not have been relied upon against him in view of the fact that he had not filed any appeal in this Court against his acquittal, and (iii) the High court was wrong in holding that the retracted Judicial confessions of accused 1 and 6 were inadmissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of the accused 5 can be relied upon by the prosecution for convicting them under section 120B read with s.120B I P. C. [799C] 2.1 The retracted Judicial confession of the appellant could not, therefore, be relied on against him. [781E F] 2(a) The retractedjudicial confession of a person accused of an offence under section 27 of the Evidence Act can be used only for corroboration in material particulars and it cannot be used as evidence against him unless he is corroborated by other independent evidence. [783F G] (b) The High court has considered the evidence and dismissed the appeal filed by the State for enhancement of sentence. [784G H] 2.(a) It is well settled that the confession of an accused person can be acted upon only if it is corroborated in material details. [779D] (c) The confession of one accused recorded under section 164 Cr. P C. and the High Courts ' dismissal of Criminal Appeal No. 38 of 1977 filed by him against his conviction and sentence are not open to challenge on the ground that they are inadmissible in material aspects. [780E F; 780B] (d) The evidence of the approver is not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appel lant accused for the murder of the deceased. [777G H, 778A] (e) The extra judicial confession made by the appellant before a Magistrate under section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act cannot be relied as against him because he had been acquitted by a High Court of the charge of conspiracy under section 307 read with sections 120B and 34 I P C., and no appeal against his acquitted was filed in this court. [771C] (f) The appellant has not filed an appeal in the Supreme Court against the acquittal of the other accused.

The appellant executed a will in favour of his father, the respondent. The testator died on August 22, 1945 and his son was brought up by his widow, the appellant. On August 22 the appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties between himself and his wife. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the will was not proved to be the last will and testament of the testator and that it was her will in the sense that it represented her intentions. Held, that the evidence of the appellant himself was considered by the learned judge and his conclusion was based on a consideration of the evidence led by him. The High Court had rightly held that there was no evidence to prove the execution of the will. The evidence of this witness was corroborated by the appellant 's case about the execution and the dispositions in the will and the evidence adduced by the respondent on the question of attestation of the Will was highly improbable. The onus was upon him to establish that the testator had really understood its contents, and he had put his signature on it when she was in a sound and disposing state of mind. The burden was on him to prove that the execution was signed by him and that he understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the document. The appellant had not discharged this onus by proving that the testatrix had really understanding its contents. The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is a rebuttable one and it would be sufficient if the Court accepts the evidence as true, but where the evidence is clear and unambiguous, the court has to accept the same and act upon it. In the present case no doubt the appellant had signed the will in his own free will but he did not at all support the appellant"s case regarding previous instructions because according to him the testatrix was in sound and disposed state of her mind and that she understood the contents of the document before she made the will, and that the signature of the testatrix on the instrument intending that the recitals and dispositions were his recitals and disposition.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arc Carbons, known as "Cinema Arcocors" and also a "component parts of motor vehicles". The goods were sold by it to various persons. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on these sales under section 3(1) (a) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant challenged the levy before the High Court. The High Court held that the main use of the are carbons was not "electrical goods" falling within entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Act and that they fell under Entry 41 of the second schedule to the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that (i) the words "electricity goods" in item 41 of Sch. 1 of Andhra Pradesh State General Sales tax Act, could not be said to have been used for goods sold for agricultural purposes merely because some of them are also sold to agriculturists for agricultural purpose; and (ii) the use of these words was not a "electric goods", falling within Entry 41, of Schedule I of the Madras General Sales Taxation Act, 1958. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The term "electronic goods" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the entry does not relate to goods sold or to agricultural purposes only but also to goods produced for agricultural pur poses. [562 E] 2. The word "electony" is employed in the Schedule to describe articles which may be manufactured for a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of apparatus would not cease to be covered by the intended entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [563 E] 3. The expression "electuring electrodes" is defined in the Act to mean "to perform any function which is necessary for the purpose of performing such functions". It will include all those items which are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. [564 G] 4. The words "required for use" in Entry 41 are used in several entries, such as entry 41, List I, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for the use as a aid or addi tion. It would be noticed from the fact that they are known as 'electrical articles ' in the market. This is evident from the words 'parts thereof '. The fact that these can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could never detract from the classification to which the carbon are belong. [565 G H] 5. The use of a are carboxydes is used as an equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The first entry in the list relates to "electorial goods" and includes "components parts thereof". The second entry also refers to "comuses" which are used for inspection, signaling, stage lights, etc. [567 G H; 565 A] 6. The definition of "electures" is given in the explanation to section 2(g) of Act. It does not refer to goods which might have been produced for use on a particular piece of instrument or for search. [568 B C] 7. The entry does relate to parts of goods manufactured for using as an assistance or addition, and it will be seen that the word "accessories" is not used in any other sense. [569 G H].

The petitioners are the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners were granted mining leases in respect of minor minerals by the State Government for the period from 1 7 1985 to 30 10 1985. The State Government issued an order on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Act amending the Gujarat Minerals (Regulation and Development) Rules, 1966 with effect from 1st July, 1985 substituting the original rule 21 of the Rules by a new rule 21. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such. [408B] 2.1 The Act has been passed for public interest and purposes by making a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the Central Government. The statute and the Rules are in the nature of subordi nate legislation. They are intended to be used for the purpose of implementing a policy of granting leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor mineral. [416C D] 2:2 In the instant case, the petitioners have not made any attempt to establish that there is any movement in the public interest. The only thing required is to see whether there is such movement as would satisfy the test of reasonableness and if so what is the purpose for which it was intended. [414D E] 3.1 It is no doubt true that the Act is passing for de pos session of minerals but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in public interest, levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. [413D E; 414E] 3:2 The Act does no doubt authorise the State Govern ment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in nature of subordinate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification in any way the freedom guaranteed under Article 301 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one state to another. [411E F] 3(a) The Act and the rules are in two parts, namely, (i) a larger restriction is imposed both on the area in respect whereof a Parwana could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there was no reasonable nexus between the classification for purpose of the proviso to Rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and Rules. [409F H] 3 (b). The fact that section 15 does no authorise the Government to show any such concession is also not of any consequence.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The office of a hereditary Trustee is in the nature of property. It is an office which is capable of being managed by a person who has no right to manage it. [445 B] (2) The expression "regulated by usage" in section 6 (9) means not hereditary but must be construed as including all persons who may have been appointed to a post in the temple. [427 C D] (3) The word "control" is used in the sense of administration of religious institutions. It includes all matters which are usually associated with religious practices and ceremonies. [416 E F] (4) The words "regulated" and "succession to this office" in the section mean that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course because the successor acquires a right only by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis. [414 D E] (5) The appellant was appointed as a hereditary trustees under section 6 of the Act. He did not hold any such post for life. It was not possible to say that there was a succession of As office to another when on the expiry of the period of one year and not for life, it was a vacancy and B is elected to that office. [413 E F; 414 A] (6) The appointment of the appellant as a temporary trustee under section 4(9), of the Tamil Nadu Act 19 Of 1951, is valid. [411 C D].

The appellant was charged under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his house in the open space where he was sleeping and when he went near his brother who was sleeping, he saw the accused running away from the place of occurrence. He was also seen by PW 4 with the appellant. The trial court acquitted the second accused but convicted him under section 201 IPC and sentencing him to death and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On appeal the High Court acquitted the third accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the testimony of PW 4 in the first information report is not a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other; (ii) the evidence of PW4 in the second information report stands contradicted by the medical evidence and (iii) the High court has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was not right in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of a single witness. [710E] 2. The evidence of the sole witness is corroborated by the contents of the FIR. The very fact that this witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. It is not possible to accept that he would not mention about this fact in the First Information Report. [ 709B] 3. The testimony of the second eye witness cannot be considered as a very weak infirmity since it has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the deceased. [610E F] 4. The mere fact that the witness has stated in the earlier report that the appellant saw PW 1 running away after the assault is true, it is difficult to appreciate how he would be able to appreciate that he could not mention the fact in his first information Report. If the statement of PW 3 is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the place where he fell dead and the deceased fell down after the attack was true, there is no reason why he would have seen that the persons who might have already escaped. [700F G] 5. The fact that PW 4 had stated in his First Information report that he saw PW1 running away while running away would not ask PW 4 to inform PW 4 who arrived at the spot a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. There is no evidence on record to show that PW4 was present at the time of occurrence when he came running. [ 700H; 700A] 6. The first information statement is true that the accused had stated that he had seen PW 1 going away from his house and running away thereafter. But the fact that he has stated that the dead body was found at No. 1 does not make any difference because the evidence in this case stands contradicted both by the testimony in court on a very material point. [1, H] 7. The statement of the first witness is not corroborated by his contents. It may be true that those who gathered would not asking PW 4, who arrived near his deceased elder brother about the accused ran away from there.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax in the hands of the Income tax Officer under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Indian Income tax Act. The respondent claimed that the amounts received by him as heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by the deceased person before his death and that the amount was liable to be assessed under section 24 B(1). The Income tax officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the payments were not taxable as they were made by the heirs and Legal representatives of the deceased Amarchand and were therefore not liable to pay out of the estate of the respondent. The Tribunal however held that these amounts were not liable for income tax under section 4(1) (b) of the Act, but only those which were received by a person who was alive. On reference, the High Court held that on a correct interpretation of section 24A the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which had been held not to be liable to tax were not exempt from income tax. The Commissioner of Income tax appealed to this Court. Held: (i) The words "or any tax which would have been payable under this Act if he had not died" in sub s.(1) of section 4 of the , are wide enough to include all persons who were alive and who could be assessed as income tax on the death of a person before the death. The expression "or other legal representatives" in section 24(B) means that the heirs or legal representatives are liable to make good any part of the income received in the previous year. (ii)The words "any person" in s.24A mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a deceased person, if the income is received by his heirs and other legal representative after his life time, they are liable for payment of tax just as the deceased would have be assessed to tax under the Act. (iii)The expression "any other legal heir" in the section means that irrespective Of the date when the income was received or the death had not taken place. The words 'or any liability which arose ' in sub sections (1), 2 and 3 of s 24B are wide and include all those who were liable to payment of income tax out of their estate. The word "person" is used in a wider sense than that of an ordinary person. In the present case the amounts were sought by the respondent as heirs of Amar Chand after his deceased life and they were therefore liable to income Tax under section 12B as his income was not taxable.

The petitioner, a member of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, were promulgated by the State Government under section 3 of the Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of these rules on the ground that they contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was not made in exercise of the power conferred by the proviso to article 309(2) of the Constitu tion. Held: (i) The word "public employment" in section 3 is used in a wide sense and includes all persons employed in any department or office under the Government of, or any local or other authority within the territory of India or Union territory. The expression "public service" in the proviso means public services and includes services which are either expressly or by necessary implication excluded from the purview of the definition. (ii)The word "Public Employment" is used to denote a group of persons who have been appointed directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the State Public Service Commission for their own benefit, and not as a matter of right. The word 'public employment ' in section 2(g) of that Act includes all non gazetted Government servants. (iii)The expression "Public employment" is not defined in the Act but has been used in the sense of employment in a department or an office under a State Government. The definition of public employment in section 4 of the , does not include employment in any other department or authority within its territory. (iv)The words "public services" in sub section (1) of section 3 are wide enough to cover all non residential persons who are employed in the State or Union Territory as a condition of employment. The words "under the Government ' to which the word is used are not defined and therefore, they cannot be construed as meaning public service.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them he was convicted under section 53 of the Act and in one of them was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court accepted the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and acquitted him of all the charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the appellant had secreted the letter just because it was found in an almirah which is said to have been in his exclusive possession, and (2) the mere fact that he was in the exclusive possession of the house and the almirah did not amount to any theft. HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the joint possession of appellant 's father and of which the key was furnished by the father. [414 D] (ii)The mere fact of seizure of the articles does not make it a case of theft. It is sufficient if the point to be established is whether the almirah was in his possession exclusively or even jointly with his father. If that is so, the taking away of the article by the appellant from the post office (if that is how he came by the articles) would be theft but it has not been found that he committed any theft and therefore the taking of the ornaments by the key is an offence under section 54 of the . [414 F G] (iii)The fact that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the appellant cannot sustain an inference that the box was in its exclusive possession. The search of the almirah is not necessary for proving that the articles were in his conscious possession. It has also to be proved that he had no knowledge of the contents of the box. [415 B] (iv)The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could have been convicted under s. 52 without the court having to consider whether he had secrets the articles.

The appellant was the Secretary of a Panchayat Samiti. The Sarpanch of the Panchayat, who had been appointed as the Chairman of the Samiti, was not present at the time when the meeting was held. He was also not prepared to go to Tehsil but was presenting before the Panchayat whatever he had got in his possession. The appellant filed an application under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Sub Divisional Magistrate staying further proceedings before him. The High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit properly sworn to or a certified copy of the order He had no opportunity to explain his conduct. [117 D] (ii) The appellant 's application for stay was not accompanied by an affidavit duly sworn to and signed by him. It was not made after the proceedings on that date had commenced. [118 E] (iii) The order sheet did not show that any application was made before the Nyaya Panchayat. No application was filed in the Court of the Nyaya panchayat, nor was there any thing in the order sheet to show that the appellant 'rejected the objections raised by the Sarpanch and inadequacy of the evidence contained therein regarding the stay order alleged to have been passed by the High Court. [119 G] (iv) The record shows that the Sarpanch had not filed an affidavit before the High Commissioner, nor did he file any affidavit in support of his allegations. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302, I.P.C., for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant at the Police Station was inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not supported by any medical evidence, and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court had been wrongly rejected by the trial court. HELD : (i) The High Courts erred in rejecting the statement of the appellant about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai. [211 G] (ii) The evidence of the approver was corroborated by the fact that he was a witness of the occurrence and his evidence was corroborated not only by the medical evidence but also by the evidence of other independent witnesses. [212 B C] (iii) The extra judicial confessions were admissible in evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act, as it was made before the Magistrate when he had given the statement to the police officer. The fact that the appellant had a bath in the Canal at that hour did not make him a witness against himself. [213 E F] (iv) The confession was corroborated in material particulars by the statements made by the accused under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the High Courts were right in rejecting it. [214 B C]. (v) The statement of an approver recorded at the police station is admissible in terms of section 32(1)(a) of the Indian Evidence Act. [216 E] (vi) The fact of the confession made to a Police Officer was not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder.

The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll of the State Legislative Assembly on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the whole election process was vitiated on the basis of the defective electoral roll. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had committed an error in not following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly dismissed the writ petition. [495C] 1.2 The High Courts have failed to follow the procedure laid down by law and have acted in a manner which is contrary to the well settled principles of natural justice. [498E] 1:3. The failure to comply with Rule 4 (1) and (2) of Rules 4(2) is fatal to the election petition. It is not the case of the petitioners that they did not know immediately after the publication of the notice under Rule4(1). They did not even know immediately thereafter when the notice was issued. [500F] 1 :4. The procedure prescribed by law for the preparation and presentation of electoral rolls is a mandatory one. It cannot be said that the failure to do so in the instant case amounts to an error on the face of record. [501A B] 1I:5. The appellants were entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the High Courts had committed no error in dismissing the petition. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. In 1949, it entered into a contract with the respondent company for the supply of electricity to its factory at Ahmedabad. The agreement provided that the Company would pay to the company Rs. 1,00,000/ per annum on or before 30 10 1967 and the balance sheet and profit and loss account would be submitted within one month from the date of commencement of the contract. In 1966, the respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 134 of the 1913 Act alleging that the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of section 220 of the 1956 Act. The trial court held that the respondent was guilty of the offence under section 135 of the Act and sentenced him to pay Rs. 2,000 as compensation for breach of contract. On appeal by the company, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and sentence and directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 3,000 to the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the failure to call a general meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit & loss account before an annual general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar; (2) the default in filing copies of the balance Sheet or the profit and Loss account before it may expose the person responsible for punishment under other provisions of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and section 220 Of the Act, and (3) the imposition of a penalty is not illegal merely because no part of the sum has been paid to the appellant. HELD: (1)(a) The failure to file the list of books and profit or loss account within the time prescribed by the respective sections of both the Acts does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of the Old Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 or of the Companies Act as the case may be. [403 B] (b) The omission to call for a general body meeting and add to the balanceheet and profit, and loss accounts before an Annual General Meeting is a circumstance which makes it punishable under sub section (3). [404 C D] (c) Section 134 lays down that after balance sheet or profit and losses account or the income and expenditure account, as the ease may be, have been laid before a general election. But section 134 lays out that after the balance has been laid up, a statement of fact and of the reasons therefore has to be annexed to the Balance Sheet and to the copies thereof required to be filed with the Registrar. [409 G H] (2)(a). The provision under section 132 of the , is for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions contained in the Act. It is not necessary that the balance should be kept separate from the balance in the balancesheet or profit & Loss account. [411 B C] (3)(b) Section 133 lays down a procedure for the preparation and publication of the accounts and the copies of balance sheet etc. before an election to fill up the vacancies.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the object of the impugned Act is to show that it is based on a reasonable classification of persons to whom or the offences in respect of which the procedure laid down in it is to apply and hence it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. The object of section 5 (1) is to provide for speedier trial of certain offences and not to punish any particular case or classes of cases or classes thereof, or class of cases as the State Government may by general or special order in writing direct. The Act does not contemplate a single trial of several offences but only one trial of all such offences. It is the State which has to make an application under section 6 (1), and it is the duty of the State to determine whether it should be tried by a Special Court, and if so, to what extent. The procedure prescribed in the Act for trial of any offence or classes or cases as laid down by it is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. The scheme of the Code of Criminal Procedure shows that the legislature has made a distinction between offences and offences under the Penal Code and those under the Indian Penal Code, and the object being to provide speediers trial for certain offences. The classification of offences or classes and the cases which in its view require speedieration is not arbitrary but must be based on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and left out. The distinction between a case and a class of offences cannot be said to be unreasonable, because, the classification has to be founded on a rational basis and it must be founded upon a reasonable basis and not on a mere possibility of an intelligible differentiation.

The appellant was a Radiologist in the Medical College of Delhi. He was appointed as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy (ex officio) both by the University of Delhi as well as by the Maulana Azad Medical College. The post of Associate Professor was advertised by the Central Health Service, Ministry of Health and Family Planning, Department of Health, New Delhi, inviting applications for the post of Assistant Professors in the said college. The appellant was selected by the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 8(2) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1965. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the selection and appointment of the appellant as Associate Professor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the teaching experience gained by the appellant was not sufficient to entitle him to be appointed to the post. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the post in question is a clinical post while that of Associate Professors of Radiology is a teaching post; (ii) the qualifications and experience prescribed for appointment to the said post are different and the appellant who had been substantively appointed to that post cannot be appointed by direct recruitment as Professor of radiotherapy or Associate Professor in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and (iii) the status of Associate professor of Radiologist cum Associate Professor is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professors in Willing don Hospital or Safdarjung Hospital and the mere designation of the said appellant as such does not give him a right to hold the post, because he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in Radiology (exclusive) in the willing don hospital or the Shahdara. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The post in dispute is a medical college and it is a post belonging to specialists Grade II. It is a research post. It has been designated as such by the university of Delhi under Rule 7(2). The appellant who was substantively appointed as Associate professor in the Irwin Hospital, has been continuously working as Assistant Professor of Pathology (Ex officio) in that hospital for over 17 years. He has been regularly appointed to this post and he is entitled to be considered for appointment by direct appointment as Professor. [802C D] 1.2 The post is a provisional one and the University can appoint an officer on probation for a period not exceeding two years. In the absence of any specific order of appointment, the appellant cannot claim to have been appointed to any post in the Institute. He had been continuously appointed as Assistant Professors of radiology (Executive) in a teaching hospital like the Irin Hospital. The fact that he was initially appointed as a Radiographer cum Associate professor on ad hoc basis does not make him eligible for appointment. [883D E] 1:3. The appointment of appellant as an Assistant Professor is not a regular appointment and his appointment cannot be challenged in any court. [894E F] 1 :4.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of workmen employed in the respondent 's region. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 95 per day. In the year 1962, the Company made an application to the Industrial Tribunal for fixation of minimum wage of the workmen and for payment of bonus on that basis. The Tribunal fixed the minimum wage at Rs. 90 per day and in respect of the same, it took into account the total number of workmen who had to be paid production bonus. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that there were other industries in the region which could be compared with the appellant 's industry in the area. [682 D] (ii) The minimum wage payable by those industries is very small and almost insignificant as compared with those in the Company 's area. In this case, however, there was nothing to show that the company was providing any amenities which were different from the amenities that are being provided by those concerns in the regions which are being used for the purpose of fixing minimum wage. [641 D] The Tribunal had rightly held that the minimum wages payable by the industries were very small. [651 E] (iii) The workmen are not providing any such amenities as are different from those that are required by those concern in the Region which are to be used for maintenance of the industry. They are not entitled to any additional benefits under the Act. [661 F] (iv) The award was made on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and there was no reason why the Tribunal should have proceeded to fix the minimum rate of wages in the company on the ground that it was based on the circumstances that, according to the workmen, the bonus in their case was being calculated as equivalent to three months ' basic wages. [671 F G] (v) The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal that there was a substantial industry in this region comparable with the Company in the other region is not correct.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was carrying on business as commission agents. The Income tax Officer issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, for the assessment year 19 19 ' and called upon him to furnish within 30 days from the date of service of the notice a return showing all or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice. The assessee filed an application under section 147 of the Act before the Income tax officer for issue of a notice on the ground that he had failed to comply with the requirements of section 148 and section 151(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Commissioner rejected the application holding that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with section 151 (2) Of the Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The notice under s 148 is valid only if it does not comply within 30 day of service. If the assessee fails to do so, the Income. tax Officer has no jurisdiction to issue a notice in respect of that period. In the present case, the assessee did not have the opportunity to make a return under section 139(2). The notice was issued on June 3, 1966 and it was served on the assessee on July 1, 1966. The notice did not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit case for issue notice under Section 148. (ii)The notice was vague and indefinite and was not in accordance with the provisions of section 151. The order sheet recording the reasons of the income tax Officer as required by section 148(2), was not produced.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in the name and style of 'M/s. Doypack Ltd., and its partners. The firm consisted of three partners, namely, (1) M/s Doyppack Ltd.; (2) M.L.A. and (3) M, L.A., and the appellant was a partner in a firm. The Income tax Officer held that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, but he did not accept the contention of the appellant that the firm had ceased to exist on April 1, 1939, and therefore the income tax proceedings were barred by section 25(3) of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant could not be said to have ceased to be a partner on April 13, 1938, and that the assessment proceedings were therefore barred by limitation under section 25 (3). HELD: (i) The question whether the business carried on at the commencement of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, was liable to tax in respect of the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such succession, is a question of fact. [107 B] (ii) The word "business" in section 25 means a business which has been carried on by a person who is carrying on any business on which tax was at any time charged under the Act of 1918. It does not mean that the income must be assessed to tax for the period during which it is charged under that Act. [108 E] (iii) The words "business or vocation" in the section are wide enough to include a business carried by a firm, and the word "income" in its ordinary sense means any business carried out on behalf of another person. The word 'business ' has been used in the context of the Act as meaning a business or profession which is carried on for profit. [109 G H] (iv) The expression "business " in section 2(4) of Income tax, 1922 includes a business of manufacture and sale of goods. It is not possible to say that the word ' business ' in section 10(3)(b) of Act of 1922, means any profession or vocation which is ordinarily carried on with profit motive. [110 G H; 111 A] (v) The definition of "business", in section 3(4), includes a firm carrying on an activity which is not merely a change in the constitution of a partnership but also a change of management. It may be that there may be a succession only to the business which had paid tax under a statute of 1918, and it may be possible that there might be a right to the benefit of section 25 in respect Of the income profits and losses of the year. But the fact that he was not taken on in the original business also shows that the original firm was not in existence at the time of the partition and therefore his income tax was payable by him. [111 B C] (vi) The mere fact that the partners were not taken into the original partnership did not make them liable to pay tax for any year. The fact that they were not taking on the original, business also does not make the firm liable to be assessed under the Income Tax Act of 1916. [112 G H].

The appellant, a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener, was born in the year 1947. He had two sons, namely, his two sons and the widow of his two daughters. The first son died in 1954. The second son died on September 1, 1956. The third son died before the coming into force of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and the appellant 's mother was the only surviving son. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the coparcenary property claiming that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary and that there were six sharers in the coparcenary properties, that there had been no prior division and that it was not possible for the appellant to get a share therein. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the property belonged to a joint family and that, therefore, there was a prior partition. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit property belonged exclusively to the Joint Hindu Mitakshara Family and that in any event, the appellant was entitled only to a half share; (ii) the respondent 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s estate upon his death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The property belonged not only to the coparcenary but also to the widow. [724B] 2.1 A joint Hindu coparcenary is a creature of statute and it cannot be created by any statute. It is not open to the Legislature to create a fictional or artificially in respect of a joint Hindu family property. [764C D] 2(a) The rule that a coparcener has to take a share only in the undivided family property, is not correct. A coparcener has no right to claim a share on partition or a share which he would have obtained if a partition of his property had taken place immediately before his death irrespective of whether he was entitled thereto at a partition or not. [774D E] 2 (b) The mere fact that the father died in 1955, does not by itself make him a coparcener. In a partition between the two sons there would be four sharers and the plaintiff 's half share therein will be 1/6th. [773G H] 3(a). The right of a Hindu coparcener to claim his share in a joint property is not a matter which can be decided by the Court on an application under Order 21, Rule 90 C.P.C. [777B] (b). In a suit based on partition between a co sharer and the other members of the family, it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step to ascertain the share, of the deceased in the coparcener 's property. It was necessary in that case to ascertain 1/4th share which the deceased had in the Mitakshara coparcenary property at the time of his death, in addition to the share that he or she received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition. [779C D; 780B] 3 (c) The right to a partition is not an absolute one and it can be exercised only by the heirs mentioned in section 6(1). [782F G] 4. In order to ascertain whether a partition had actually taken place between the plaintiff and his two brothers, there would have been four sharer in the family property each having one share in it.

The respondent was appointed as a Class II employee in the appellant Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Manager (General) on or before 31st October, 1956 and was confirmed with effect from 1st November, 1956 by an order dated 30th April, 1957. The respondent challenged the said order by a writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same holding that the employees of Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on and after 1 st September,1956 were not entitled to continue in service beyond 60 years as they had been promoted to a class I post. The appellant Corporation filed an appeal before this Court against the said decision. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court erred in striking down regulation 19(2) of the Staff Regulations, 1960 as amended in 1976 and in directing the Corporation to continue the 1st Respondent in its service till he completed 58 years of age. [223G] (2) The order of the High court is set aside and the appellant corporation is directed to continue him in service till 60 years of his age. The Corporation shall continue the respondent in its employment till he completes 58 years. [225B C] (3) The respondent was not entitled for any reduction of the age of retirement from 60 years to 58 years on their being promoted to Class I post or class II post. [226C D] (4) The appellant corporation should have been directed to pay to the respondent salary at the rate of Rs.400 p.m. from 1.9.1956 till he attained the age 55 years.

The appellants, who were the Judges of the High Court, filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of the Full Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the contempt proceedings were not maintainable as the appellants had never been given notice of any contempt. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letter was addressed by a person who was not in keeping with the well accepted role of a Judge and prestige of the profession to which the deponent had the honour to belong, and therefore the apology was not bona fide. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contempt proceedings are dropped. [243E] 2. The letter dated 20 February 1975 addressed by the appellant to the President of India cannot be construed as scandalising the Hon 'ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. [244B C] 3. The appellant tendered his apology to this Hon ' ble Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance. The Full Bench was wrong in accepting the apology without finding that the appellants committed any contempt of court. [245E F] 4. The apology is not a part of the duty of a judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a Judges to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. [246F] 5. The question whether the appellants commit any contempt or not does not arise for consideration in this case. The matter did not constitute any contempt and the appellants were guilty of contempt of Court. [247C D] 6. The respondents had committed contempt of a court by publishing false statements in their own hand. They had no intention to scandalise the court. They were guilty under section 2(c) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. [248D E] 7. The appellants had not been given any notice of contempt. It is only when the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court would take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. [249E F; 250A] 8. The Court had no power to punish a person for contempt of its own or of the Hon"ble Judges or to lower the authority or to undermine the prestige of its profession. [250B C, H] 9. The court has no power under section 19(1) (b) of that Act to punish any Judge who is guilty of any offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years. [251C] 10. The word " contempt" in section 19 (1)(b) means an act done by a judge in his own interest in the discharge of his judicial duties. It does not mean that the act must be done in good faith and with due care and caution. [252E F, H; 252A] 11. The expression "any other cause" in the section means any act or omission which is calculated to prejudice the interests of the public in general. [253G] 12. The words "any act or default" in sub section (1) of section 19 are wide enough to include an act or failure to comply with the provisions of the Act. [254B C; 255A B] 13. The use of the word "may" in clause (b), in the context of which it is used, indicates that there is a presumption of guilt of contempt against the Judge. The presumption of innocence is not absolute and the court has to be satisfied about the existence of such a presumption. [255C D; 255D] 14.

The petitioner, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49 under the Indian Income tax Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore not saved by article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of section 6(5) of Act XXXV of 1947 were valid and did not contravene article 14. The procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affected the petitioner was a reasonable restriction within the meaning of article 19 (1)(f) of India. The impugned Act was therefore void. The provisions of the impugned section were not discriminatory and could not be said to offend article 14, because, under the provisions Of section 5 (1) the procedure prescribed in the impugned sections was a good substitute for that prescribed by Indian Income Tax Act. Held further, that section 6 (5) was valid as it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Part III of the constitution. The object of the section was to provide for the imposition of reasonable restrictions on the right to carry on business in India and to make provision for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. The Act did not violate article 14 because, it contravened the provisions contained in article 19(6) of that Article. The classification made by the Act was based upon a rational basis and was not arbitrary or irrational. The fact that under the Act the procedure to be followed for catching evaded income was a relevant consideration for determining whether the assessee had evaded payment of tax would not make any difference, because the procedure laid down in section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act is a reasonable one and does not offend article 19.

The Federation was established by an agreement dated January 21, 1956 with its members. The terms of the agreement were to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The respondent No. I was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. It had its registered office at Delhi. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act and having its registered address at New Delhi, was carrying on business in the premises in question. The Company was established for the purpose of promoting the trade of the Federation or any part thereof for such consideration as the Federation may think fit and in particular for shares, debentures, etc. The members of the appellant 's Association were also members of a registered society known as "Ambalal" which was registered under section 2 (1) of that Act. The Society was registered on January 21. 1956. The Registrar of Shops and Establishments, Delhi issued notices to the Federation calling upon it to show cause why its establishment should not be terminated for breach of conditions of service of its members and also for payment of compensation for loss or damage caused by such termination. The Association filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the activities of the respondent No 1 were not "business" within section 2 of the . In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The activities of respondent No I were not 'business ' within the definition of " commercial establishment". [356 F] (ii) The activity of respondent 1 was in nature of a business or trading and it was immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial Establishment". It is immaterial whether the activities bring the premises within that category or a 'commercial establishment '. [356 G] (iii) The definition of 'business" in section 2,(5), does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Federal Court inR. K . Of course that profit was plouGDhed back. [337 B C] (iv) The word "business ' does not mean anything by which an activity carried on by it amounts to a busi (1)[1971] 1 S.C.R.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his brothers. The income from the agricultural land was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Income tax Officer held that it had been a regular assessment of the income and did so on the ground that it could not be said that the receipt of the asses see was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. The High Court in reference held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The source of the allowance or pension is the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore, it is not agricultural income as defined in section 2(1)(a) of Act. [702 D] (ii) The words "income from land" are used in the definition in section 4 (3)(vii) of Income tax, 1922, and they are not defined in the Act, but in the Indian context. [700 E] (iii) The income of a person is derived from land which is used for agricultural purposes. It is not an income derived from lands used for agriculture. [602 G] (iv) The High Courts were right in holding that from a reading of the letters of July, 18 37, it was clear that the source of income was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of his income was not land or rent collections from land, it could be said to have been the immediate sources of the pension.

The petitioners in C.A. No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors Grade II in different ordnance factories between 1962 and 1966 a nd they were promoted as Chargeman II on the basis of selection list prepared in the manner provided therei n, but their promotion was not made on completion of two years ' service as Supervisor 'A. The petitioners filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the order dated 28th December 1965 and the circular dated 20th January 1966 which superseded the earlier circular dated 6th November 1962 and had provided that in future promotions of all such individuals will be effected in accordance with the normal rules and not merely on the completion of one year 's service. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners were on the same footing as those who had been promoted as Supervisor Grade II on expiry of 2 years of continuous service on the ground that they had completed two years of service as Supervisors 'A ' by its order dated 16th April, 1979 and that it was not disputed that all of them have in due course be promoted as chargeman II with effect from the date their juniors were promoted. In the writ petition filed by the petitioners challenging the said order of the High Court, this Court held that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to issue any direction for automatic promotion merely on completion o f 2 years ' servi ce as Supervisor A ' and that the circular of 20th February 1966 was superseded by the circular issued in the case of the petitioners. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellants that after the issue of the subse quent order dated 6 th November, 1962 no Supervisor 'B ' could claim to have been promoted merely on completing 2 years service as a person will not be entitled to any salary and allowance during the period for which he did not actually possess the duties of a higher post although after due consideration he was given a proper place in the gradation list prepared by the State Government. Dismissing the appeals, this court, HELD: 1. The order dated 2nd February, 1981 is completely silent on the point and the appeal has been filed only on the question of seniority. [408C] 2. The appellants of this appeal have in pur poses of the orders passed by the High court of Madhya Pradesh and the legal consequences flowing therefrom. [409D] 3. The State Government has no power to issue a direction for regular promotion merely because it is found that the appellants had been given due consideration for promotion. It is not open to the Court to speculate on the subsequent order dated 20 th January, 1966 as to whether it was in any way contrary to law or otherwise. [411E] 4. The judgment of this Court dated 2 nd February,1981 in C A No. 442 of 1981 in C P No. 971 of 1981 is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. [413F] 5. The respondents have in their counter affidavit stated that the State has no authority to issue such direction for regularisation merely on expiry o f two years service. It was also stated that it would be appropriate that the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 440 of 1981 may also be granted the same relief which was granted to the petitioners in the writ peti tion before the Madhya Pradesh High Court. [414F G] 6.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (K.S.R.T.C.) was constituted under the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to carry out the purposes of the Act. The Regional Transport Authority and the High Court held that the State Transport Undertaking would have preference over all eligible applicants for permits from the State transport undertaking. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Karnataka Road Transport Corpora tion (K S.R.) would have priority over other applicants who had applied for permits under section 47(1 H) of the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1984 and that the said preference would be given to those applicants who were not eligible for permits since they did not possess a valid permit from the Regional Transport Authorities. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Karnataka State Transport Undertakings (Ks. R.T.) Corporation (KSRTC) is an instrumentality of the State and it has been established that there are several private operators in the State. It is also established that the transport undertaking would have a monopoly. [1015G] 2. Section 47(i H) provides that where, in pursuance of an approved scheme, a State Transport undertaking applies for a stage carriage permit, a contract carriage permit or a public carrier 's permit in respect of a notified area or notified route, such permit shall be granted to the State Government by the State Road transport Corporation in a case where the said area or route lies in more than one region and the Regional transport Authority in any other case. [1005A B] 3. The scheme of the Karnataka State Undertaking would show that except in the case of a specified category, all other applications for permits are to be considered on merits. [105C D] 4. Section 48(1) provides for preference over other applications. It also provides that preference shall be given in favour of applicants who have applied for a permit from any State Transport Authority. The expression "preference" is not defined in the Act, but it has to be understood in its ordinary sense as meaning "a person who has been granted a permit". [1016E F] 5. Section 68F(1)(b) provides a special procedure for grant of stage carriage permits. It does not say that the permit shall he granted to a State transport Undertaking. The reference to Chapter IV A there was for the purpose of comparisoning the exclusion contemplated by section 68F. [102H; 103A] 6. Section 49(1), however, provides that in the cases of inter State route, the permits may be granted either absolutely or subject to any rules that may be made under this Act. [103B C] 7. The word "preferably" is used in the context of section 47 (1 H). It does mean that where a permit has been issued by an authority not competent to grant it, it will have to be construed as having regard to the provisions of the statute and the rules framed thereunder. [104C D; 105E] 8. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the State Appellate Tribunal have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Mysore State Road Trans port Corporation and the private operators who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government, because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to section 63(7). [105E] 9. The High Court has overlooked the fact that the permits to be granted are for tourist vehicles, and the preference provided for by clause (iv) and to be given under section 48(l H) is confined only to operators of tourist cars and travel agents. [106F G] 10. The Tribunal and High Court have failed in considering the merits and the claims made by the Karnataka state Road Transport Undertakings. [107G] 11.

The respondent was a dealer in business of selling goods. The appellant, who was the registered owner of the business, sold the goods to the respondent on October 5, 1956 and the sale proceeds were credited into the account of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for arrears of sales tax due from him on the ground that he had purchased the goods from the State Government as a dealer under section 19(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act 1939 (Madras Act IX of 1939). The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in second appeal confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that Rule 21 A is ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Govern ment under section19(1)(a) of Madras General sales Tax Act, 1939 (Mad. IX of 1940), as amended by the Madras Act IX Of 1939). HELD: The High Court was right in holding that Rule21 A is intra vires of section 10 of the Act. [665 B] In the context and background of other sections of the .the word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 23A is beyond the rule made by the State Legislature under section 9(1). [665 C] The High Courts have rightly held that Rule 22 is ultra rites of the Rule making power and the State has no authority under its rule making powers under section 20(2)(C) of Act. Therefore, Rule 21A is ultra vivos of the rules making power.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the State of Saurashtra. He was dismissed from service on February 2, 1955. The respondent filed an application under section 33(2) (a) of the Bombay Civil Services Act, 1946 for a declaration that he continued to be in Government service till the date of his dismissal and for a decree for Rs. 1,000/ . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311(2). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts erred in holding that there was a breach Of article 311 (2) of Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against him. HELD: The High Court erred in ordering a decree under section 31(2)(a) for Rs, 1,006/ . [922 D] The State of Bombay vs The Province of Bombay, ; , referred to. (1) The provisions of article 310(2), which are mandatory and not directory, do not apply to the case of arrears of salary earned by a public servant for the period that he was actually in office. It is true that the word 'actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in section 60 of the Act does not include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of pay, the decree more properly falls under section 61(2); it is true, as held by this Court in State of Tripura vs The province of East Bengal, (1962) Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, that the words 'action able wrong other like breach of contracts ' in article 311 must be construed in their widest sense and not in narrow or technical sense. [923 D E] (2)(i) The expression 'actionabilityable wrong ' is wide enough to include all kinds of acts which have a direct bearing on the question whether they are done in good faith or for a collateral purpose. It does not mean merely that there must be some act which has a direct impact upon the right of the person who seeks relief. [948 E] In the present case, the respondent was not concerned with the second contention but it is a dispute between the State and the appellant. The State had the authority to provide the appellant with a copy or the report. The appellant was not in any way concerned with this matter. [947 G H] (ii) The decree of the High court decreeing payment of arrears for the time during which he has served was not challenged by the respondent.

The appellants were adjoining colliery owners at Kujama. The respondents claimed that the suit was not barred by limitation and they had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the alleged encroachment only within three years thereof. The trial court held that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion of the encroached area. On appeal, the High Court confirmed this finding. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts were in error in holding that the onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on the appellant; that the courts below had wrongly held that they had not given any such notice as required by section 80 C.P.C. and that the appellants had failed in their attempt to prove the fact that the respondent had knowledge about the encroachment only in the year 1941, which was within three yea years of the date of the filing of the suit; that no plan had been annexed to the lease deed executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding on the assumption that the initial burden of proof was on respondents. [497 C] (ii) Under section 80(1)(c), the court has power to require any person who is aggrieved by an order made under that section to produce evidence, and it is not necessary for a party to show that he had knowledge or had reason to believe that the order was erroneous. The onus of proving knowledge on him lies upon the party who seeks to rely on the record. [498 E] (iii) Under the rules framed by the High court under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the respondents could request the mining authorities to exempt them from the operation of rule 76 of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946 and if they wanted to remove the coal left by the appellant in the encroached land, they were bound to produce the evidence.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The respondent terminated the services of the appellant under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The appellant challenged the termination on the ground that it was mala fide and was not bona fide. The tribunal held that the action taken by the appellant was bona fide and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power conferred. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to inquire into the causes that led to termination of service under r 18(b).
