The Tribunal has the right to inquire whether there was in fact misconduct or not and if it is satisfied that the act done by the employer was a colourable exercise of power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [824 D] (ii) The appellant had failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of its power was bona bonafide and was in public interest. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding that the order terminating the services was bona fides. [884 E F] (iii) The employer could defend the action under r, 18(1) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and therefore the action was bona bona fide or was a result Of victimisation or improper unfair labour practices. [894 G H] (iv) The question whether the action of the employer in terminating the service of an employee is bona fide must be determined on the facts of each case. In the present case, the employer wanted to take action for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. But the tribunal held, that the discharge was mala fides and therefore it considered that no inquiry should be held. [904 A B] (v) The fact that the proposed inquiry is not held by the appel lant and action was taken under r 17(a), does not make any difference. The employer can take action only if there is a misconduct or misconduct on his part and if the termination of services is found to be mala fide or as result of unfair labour procedure, it will have jurisdiction.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit against the appellant defendant for declaration that he was entitled to a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the respondent was a lessee or not is one of fact depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. [445 B] (ii) The High Court has recorded a finding that the agreement was of the nature of a lease and that the consent decree operated as res judicata. [427 C D] (iii) The trial judge had rightly held that the respondent 's suit was barred by the principle of res judicata under section 92 of the Evidence Act, because the question was already concluded by the consent decrees in suit No. 149 of 1960. [416 G H] (iv) The finding of the High court is set aside and the matter remitted to the trial judge for fresh disposal according to law. [414 C D]. (v) The respondent 'could not lead any evidence to show that the document dated December, 1, 1954 was a lease. The question was never raised in the trial court or before the High Courts. [413 E] (vi) The suit was not barred by res judicata because the issue was already decided by consent decree in suit NO. 149/ 1960. The respondent could not lead evidence to prove that the said document dated November 27, 1954 created a lease, and that it had been executed by him.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was confirmed on 1st June, 1983. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer in the year 1972. The petitioner challenged his appointment by filing a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was enti tled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th August, 1985. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and directed the effect that the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled for remain in service till 30th of August,1985 and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The State filed an appeal before this Court contending inter alia that the interim order passed by the High court on 10.7.86 could not be sustained and the Writ Appeal was liable to be dismissed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3.1988 directed that the respond ent should be reinstated with full back wages. [243E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not urged before the Court that the order was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30.8. 1985 were liable to he ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. His only case was that the ad hoc order dated 10. 785 could not have been passed by him on 29.3 .1988 because his term of office had come to an end on 30th September, 1985 and no further order of extension of service could be passed by any authority. [244E G] 1:3. The respondent was not satisfied with the order allowing the Writ Petitioner as stated above. He proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be re spondent for reinstatement in service notwithstanding the fact that his term had come about on 30. August, 1984 and no order of re sion had been passed till 30st of August 1985. His case was not covered by any decision of this Court. [245E] 2.1 In the circumstances, the High Courts were justified in setting aside orders dated 24th March, 1988 and 26th July, 1988 passed by them on review and restore the Judgment dated 24 3 1988 passed in the Writ petition. [246F G] 2:2.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for seven years. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the evidence of P. 1 to 3 was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] (2) In a case where two views are possible, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the possibility of duality of views. [369F] (3) The evidence of the eye witnesses has been corroborated by the evidence given in Court of Sessions. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [370G] Khem Karan & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. (4) The fact that the appellant was a woman of 69 years old, cannot be a ground for rejecting her evidence on the basis of the statement of P W. 1. [367A B] Khem Raj & Anr. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors., ; and Khem Karan vs State, ; , applied. (5) In the instant case, the High Courts have rightly rejected the evidence on this point. [366B C] Khem Chand & Ors vs State Of U. P., ; ; Khem Karan and Ors. v State of UP. ; , ; Khem Raj vs State o/o Delhi, ; and Hari Singh & Anr vs State (Delhi Administration), ; , relied upon.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as an Assistant Sessions Judge in January, 1978. He was removed from his office by an order dated May 27, 1978 passed under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court on various grounds including that he had been removed from service without holding any inquiry or giving him a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and that the order was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) Section 6(i)(c), specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 5 of the Act alleged to have been committed by a public servant i.e. the Judge of a High Court, except with the previous sanction of the Central Government; and (ii) that the provisions of sections 6(2) and 6(3) are not applicable to the case of a Judge who is removed from office by the President in accordance with clause (4) of Article 124 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power to punish a Judge under section 3(i) of Prevention of corruption Act,1947 is a special law enacted by Parliament under Article 124(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [216C D] 1.2 The word "court" in section 6 (i)(a) has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of competent authority under Section 6 of the . [217D E] 1:3. The word 'court ' is not defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure but it has been used in the sense in which it is used in section 2(g) of that Act. It has been held by this Court in State of Bombay vs Purushottam Jog Naik, ; , that a Judge or Chief Justice of a District Court cannot be removed from the office by any other person except by his removal from office in accordance With clause (a) of article 124 and (b) a special procedure enacted by the Parliament under article 124(4) is clearly visualized when the purported misbehaviour is dealt with by the Chief Justice. [217E F] 1 :4. The provisions contained in clauses 4 and 5 of Article 125 read with Article 2(h) of Constitution are clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior judge, except by their removal from his post in the manner prescribed. [218H; 218A] 1 5. The words 'any person ' in clause (e) of sub section (1) of Section 6 are clear enough to place the onus on the accused, howsoeverlightened, to prove that he has committed a corrupt practice within the meaning of the said clause. [220B C] 1 6. The expression "any person" in clause(e) has been deliberately used by the legislature to mean only persons who have been convicted of an offense under the Act and not those who are convicted of any offence under the Penal Code.

The appellant was a Sunri by caste. He challenged the election of the respondent to the State Assembly on the ground that he belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with the Sunri caste. The Tribunal held that the appellant belonged to the "Scheduled Caste" and not to a member of any Scheduled Caste. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decision of the Tribunal and directed the election petition to be dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was not a member in the "scheduled caste" but was only a member belonging to a smaller caste group of Sahas; (ii) the Tribunal had wrongly held that item 40 excluded from the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 and, therefore, the appellant could not be said to belong to the Schedule Caste specified by item 40. HELD: (i)(a) The Tribunal was right in holding that item No. 40 had excluded from "Scheduled Castes" the Scheduled Tribe specified in items 40 and 41. [390 D] (b) The word "schedule caste" has been used in a wide sense to include all persons who belonged to a particular caste but not those who belonged either to a group of such castes or groups within the bigger caste. Therefore, the Tribunal was wrong in holding the appellant to be a member from the " Scheduled Caste" specified in Item 40. [391 C] (c) The expression "Scheduled Tribe" has not been defined in the Act and therefore it cannot be said that the word "Scheduled Tribes" has any meaning. [392 E] (d) The definition of "Scheduled caste" is a broad and general one and includes all persons belonging to Scheduled Castes or groups mentioned in item No 40. Therefore the Tribunal thought that the effect of the item was to exclude from the Sunari caste those who were belong to a larger caste group. [393 G H] (e) The appellant had not established that he belongs to the Scheduled Castes specified in the item. He did not, therefore. fall within the definition of 'Scheduled Caste '.

The appellant was the tenant of a monthly rent of Rs. 2,000 and the respondent landlord paid him the sum of Rs 29,500 to the appellant as advance payment. The appellant refused to accept the amount on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to pay the balance due in respect of the furniture and the documents that were handed over to him by the appellant. The Magistrate held that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 19(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. On appeal the Presidency Magistrate acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 20(1)(a) of that Act. The High Court on a reference made to it by the Presidency Magis trate held that there was no relinquishment of tenancy and that the document did not create any relinquishment. Held, that the word "relinquishment" in section 18 (1) (a) meant only an assignment of the tenancy and not a relinquishment. The word "distin quently" used in section 17(2), therefore, must be read as referring to an assignment by the tenant or tenant of his rights as such. The words "conveyed" in the Transfer of Property Act would have been more appropriate if the transfer was meant by surrender by the lessee or tenant. The intention of the legislature was that the transferee should have the right to receive the rent and not the relinquishment. In the present case there was a relinquishment of the rights of the appellant and therefore the transaction was one for the recovery of arrears of rent.

The appellant, a contractor, was awarded a contract for the supply of certain specified items of iron and steel. The workmen were paid Rs. 150/ per month as compensation. The dispute between the parties related to the fixation of wages at Rs.150/ in the category of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in that category. The Tribunal held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the new wage scales had been fixed with reference to the old wage scales and that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the old wages scales were just and reasonable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award of the Industrial Tribunal is set aside and the workmen are entitled to get a flat increase of Rs. 250/ in category of Draftsmen and RS. 150 per month in the case of other categories. [306G] 2.1 The new wage scale had necessarily to be fixed with flat increase in each category. If, as the Tribunal has stated in the amendment order, the increase in the basic pay of individual workman was intended to apply to each individual workmen, there is nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales can be made to rest. [307H; 307A] 2:2 The Tribunal was betrayed by a strange confusion in accepting the plea of the union that a flat increased to the pay of each workman was meant in the original wage and, therefore, it fell into the error of amending the award. [308B C] 3.1 In the case where the Tribunal had stated in its amendment order that an all round flat increase would increase to Rs.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948. Its workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 10/ per day and a piece of cloth was supplied to them by the respondent company. The company paid its employees only As. /10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The appellant contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant not to pay the wages. The authority did not decide the said question as a preliminary issue because it held that section 2(vi) included wages prescribed by the award. The Authority did not decided the said issue as a final one, but directed the appellant company to pay wages at rates fixed by the Industrial Tribunal. The respondents contended before this Court that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 10 of the , and that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. HELD: (i) The authority had found that section 3(vi)(a) included Wages prescribed by an award could not be included. [426 B] (ii) The provisions of section 2 (vi) are applicable to the case because, in reality, the wages prescribed under the award cannot fall within the definition prescribed by section 2.(vi). Therefore, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribe by the Act can not be treated as wages under section 2. [420 C] (iii) The words "any award" and "any order" in section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act are wide enough to include wages prescribed for any award. [416 D] (iv) The definition of wages prescribed in an award cannot be construed as a contract between the parties because that, in truth, is the effect of industrial adjudication. That being so, it was difficult to subscribe to the contention that the wage prescribed by award could be treated only as wages for purposes of section 22(vi).

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409, Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the trial court. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish an offence either under section 465 or section 409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for prosecuting him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction under s. 197(l) of Code of criminal Procedure was not necessary for prosecution under section 120B, Indian penal Code and that the sanction was necessary only when the act complained of attached to the official character of the person doing it, and (ii) the trial was vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 197 (1) Of the Code. HELD : (i)(a) The sanction under sub s.(l) is not required for prosecution of a public servant under section409 or section 420 of the Indian Penal code. It is only when it is shown that the act alleged to have been done by the accused person while he was actually engaged in the performance of official duties, that the offence may be said to have taken place within the scope of his official duty if his act is such as to lie within the meaning of section 409 or section 465 of the Penal Code. [1305 D E] (b) The question whether sanction under sec. 197 (l) was necessary in a case falling within the purview of section 196(1), is one which falls squarely within the ambit of his duties and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. If sanction under that section is necessary, it would not be necessary to consider whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction but is not an issue between the prosecution and the accused. [1406 F G] (c) The provisions of s.197(l)(a), Cr. P.C., do not apply to cases where the official act complained against is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have done by him under the office, then sanction would be necessary; and that would be so irrespective of whether it was, in fact, a proper discharge of his duty. [1506 G H] (d) The section does not require that sanction should be obtained for prosecution against a public officer or servant who is concerned with the official duties. It only requires that sanction must be obtained by the authority concerned and not by the Government. [1607 B C] (e) The fact that the appellant did claim to have paid the amount to Parma, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there was in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name does not make any difference.

The appellant, a resident of Travancore State, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that it had been carrying on business in British India and its business in Travancore was not exempt from tax. The Income tax Officer held that the business losses incurred in the erstwhile State of Travancore were taxable as income under section 3 Of the Indian Incometax Act, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the definition of total world income in section 2(c) of the Indian Act did not include business losses and therefore the business loss incurred in Travancore State could be set off against profits made in British Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Act; (ii) that the expression " business " in section 3 of the Travancore Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, was not used in the sense in which it was used in section 24(1)(Per Bose J.) and the proviso to section 24 (1) (Per Bose jj. The High Court held that there was no ambiguity in the definition and that the word " business" in section 10 meant only business in India and not in British England; (iii) that under the Travancore Act, income from business in an Indian State could not be set apart for purposes of computing the rate of tax on the profits made by a resident in the Indian State. Held: (i)(Per BOSE J.) (1)(a) The word "business" in the section means business in the taxable territory or to take in any other part of it, and does not include any business which is carried on in India. (b)The expression "business " in the context of the main enactment includes business in a foreign State or in an I Indian State and therefore it cannot be said that the words " business in any year" in sub section (2) of section 24 must mean business in that year. (ii)(a)(iii) The mere fact that the term " income " is not used does not justify the construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising in Indian States even to business, profession or vocation. (iv)The word " income" in s.3 of the Taxation Act means business as in the case of a resident ' total income. The mere use of the words loss of profits or gains to be set aside under section 24 is not sufficient to restrict its scope and that intention was to limit the setoff of profits arising in India only to businesses or to modification the mode or computation under s.10 of the Incometax Act.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1952 under which it had its registered office at Calcutta. The age of retirement for workmen in all industries should be 60 years subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age was extended to 58 years subject, inter alia, to 58. The company also agreed that the age shall be 60. The workmen 's case was that they were not entitled to any gratuity on the ground that they had been paid in the Bombay region. The Tribunal found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region there was no uniform practice of fixing retirement at 60 years and that the trend was to fix the retirement age at 60. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has not committed any error in holding that the conclusion recorded by this Court in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in Bombay Region had been correct. [415 D] (ii) The award and agreements on the question of age of superannuation about which information is furnished by the several documents on this record clearly shows a consistent trend in the Madras region to fix retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60, and that there was good ground for thinking that the industry cum region basis had been to fix such retirement at 58. [427 G H] (iii) The trend that has been adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable. What the Tribunal has failed to notice is that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an earlier occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. [315 D E] (iv) The approach adopted by this Tribunal in considering the question as to whether the conclusion of this Court should be accepted or not is erroneous. [416 A B] (v) The fact that the Industrial Tribunal has found that the past trend was not to fix a retirement age for workmen at 55 or 58 is an irrelevant circumstance and it cannot be said that its present conclusion is incorrect.

The first respondent, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was appointed as the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company. The first respondent filed an application before the Chairman for appointment of the second respondent as the chairman of the board of directors of the Company. The Chairman also stated that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of the appellant was being conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members and other persons and further that the persons concerned in the management of the affairs of the companies had in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. The second respondent contended that the Board could not pass an order under section 237(b) of the Act as the first respondent was not a member of the public. The third respondent also contended that there was no material before the Board on which it could and did form the opinion that there had been any fraud, faith or other misconduct against the company or towards the Company and its member. Held: (i) The power conferred on the Chairman by section 237 (b) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the company Law Board is administrative, that it can be validly exercised by the Chairman only if he has reason to believe that the circumstances suggest any of these things and not whether they establish any of those things. In the present case the first Respondent had not disclosed anything from which it can legitimately expect that the company law Board would have appointed him as the sole judge of the question whether the circumstances suggested by the appellant were sufficient to warrant an investigation into the affairs. (ii) The order passed by the first respond ent was invalid because there was ample material before him on which he could form the belief that there existed a case against the appellants and its officers. The order was therefore invalid. (iii) The Board was not empowered to delegate its function under section 236(b). The power of the Chairman to order investigation and delegation of functions is administrative in character and that it could be validly exercise by the Board but it had no power to authorise the Chairman or any other person to sub delegate this function to himself. (iv) The first Respondent was not an officer of the Government and therefore, the order was invalid.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to three years rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act had not been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, according to the prosecution, and therefore the appellants were themselves the dacoits. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the appellants had failed to establish their complicity in the crime of dacoity and therefore they could be convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code. [724 D] In the present case the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen. The appellants had been rightly convicted under sections 395 and 412 of the I.P.C. [700 G H] The High 'Court was right that the sentence of three years ' rigorous imprisonment should be reduced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment, but not of fine. [624 D E] In this case the appellants did not have any explanation for their having committed the crime. They were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits and had looted the property. The house of 20 persons was searched and large quantities of cloth were found in their houses. It is difficult to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of theft or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'thinner ' in the country, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to include in the list of substances included in the Rules as "poppy arsenic" and enabled State Government, by Rule 13 thereof, to declare any substance as poison for the purposes of the Act. The petitioners contended that since the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory treatment as it is left to each State Government not to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance as medicine was not automatically made applicable to other States. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of the enactment is to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances were included in it. The Act is intended to regulate its import, possession, sale and disposal of poisonac in which the use of such poison for purposes of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the posses sion thereof desirable. If the Government thought in the circumstances that the possi sion or sale of the same is to be regulated it could not be said that they have no power to regulate. [222C D] 2. The expression "polysenic", the expanded words are used in a sense similar to those used in the Act, and the object of which is to control the poss ession thereof desirable, is to render provision for regulating the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which it is intended. [223D] 3. The purpose of the legislation is to ensure that the possession and disposal in the area is not restricted to the quantity of poison and consequential amendment of rules 12 and 13 of the Rules. [225E] 4. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance which it considers as poison, for the entire country. It states that the State Govern ment may by rule regulate the import, Possession and sale or sale to be regulating the possibil ty of any particular poison in a local area. [226F] 5. The Government may by Rule regulate the possession or sale or disposal of any substance specified as poison in the rule. But it does not follow that the Government can regulate the posse sion for sale and the sale of such an substance. It is only when the Government thinks in the circum stances that the Possession or sale is to he regulated, it could be said to have no authority to regulate; but if the Government felt that the possess ment or sale was to be governed by a notification under the Act or the rules made thereunder, the Government could not say that they had no power. [227G H] 6. The State Government may in exercise of this power rule regulate its posses tions for sale or the sale to the specified poison. It does not mean that they are not entitled to regulate but only those substances which the Government consider it fit to do. [228A B] 7.

The assessee firm was carrying on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal for a statement of case on the following question: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the assessee in their books of account as irrecoverable in the books of accounts was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" The High Court answered the question in favour of the Department and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: (1) the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending, and (2) the Tribunal had erred in disallowing the claim of the appellant for the balance of Rs 2, 68,385. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has found that the monies were not loans made in the ordinary course of business of appellants ' firm. [10 E] (ii) The finding of the Tribunal is binding on this Court and it cannot be said that the Tribunal erred in allowing the claim for the entire amount. [11 D] (iii) The expression "accommodation" has been defined in section 10(2)(xi) to mean any accommodation, building or other thing which is capable of being used as a means of livelihood by manual labour or mechanical power. It does not include any kind of business. [12 E F] (iv) The word 'accommodity ' has been used in the context of section 10 (2)(xii). The expression 'accommodation ' has to be understood in its ordinary sense and it is not possible to define with precision all kinds of property or things which are capable of enjoyment by a person. [13 E F; 14 A] (v) The term "accommodation" has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules made thereunder. It has been understood in several decisions of this Court that the word 'incommodation ' is used in contradistinction to a mere book entry and it has been held by this Court in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs M/s. Amarchand Sobhachand, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, that the expression "commodity" has to take its colour from the context in which it occurs and must be understood as a whole. The word "accrespass" is used with reference to a thing or thing which may be done by a man in his own right. [14 E F]. (vi) The definition of 'acc abductation ' in section 2(xi) of the Income tax Act, 1922, does not mean that a debt is a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. It is not necessary to decide whether it is a loan or a debt which is owed in the normal course of the money lending.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was brought into force on September 20, 1977. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the said order of the High Court dated August 14, 1984. The said special leave petition was dismissed by a Division Bench of that High Court on April 29, 1987. In these two writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the acquisition on the ground that they were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. [565E] 2. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time or not is a matter which has to be decided by the court on the basis of the evidence and materials placed before it. [567F] 3. In the instant case, the respondents have failed to make out any case for interference with the acquisition proceedings. [568G] 4. The Special Leave Petitioners are approaching this Court for such relief must come with clean hands. They have not approached this Court with clean hand and they have not suppressed material facts. [569F] 5. The High Court has granted interim stay of dispossession in respect of the said lands. It is well settled that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court seeking such relief should come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [570F] 6. The order granting interim stay is not a direction for continuance of the proceedings till the disposal of the Special leave petition. It does not amount to suppression of material facts or there was no concealment of material fact. [571G H] 7. The petitioner has failed to show that the stay order was made within time. If the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit, they have failed in their defence. They are liable to pay compensation for the delay caused by them. [573F G] 8. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression or suppression of facts, and his application was liable to he dismissed. If this be so, the petitioner who approach this Court in an appropriate case for such reliefs must come within the ambit of the relief which is discretionary.

The appellant, a workman in the respondent Bank, was appointed as an Assistant Manager on January 1, 1959. He was drawing basic pay at Rs. 400 per month and was getting a salary of Rs. 100 per month. The appellant 's services were terminated by the respondent bank with effect from January 1. 1962. The respondent bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the workman had not been given any opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken against him and that he was entitled to increments under sub cl. (b) of cl. 100 of the Sastry award. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not given an opportunity to explain his conduct before terminating his services and that the termination was illegal as the workman did not give any opportunity of being heard before terminating the services of the respondent. HELD: (i) The respondent Bank had no right to terminate the services without giving any opportunity for showing cause against termination of service. [901 B] (ii) The appellant had no power under cl. 10(b) to terminate his services without assigning any reason. The procedure prescribed by cl. 12 is followed in the present case. [936 C D] (iii) The award was not a speaking one and it did not deal with the merits of the case. It merely dealt with the question whether the workman was entitled or not to be paid increments under the Sastry Award. The award did not say that the workmen were entitled to increment under sub cls. (a), (b), (c) and (d). [936 D] In the present cases, the respondent had no opportunity of showing cause for his termination of services. He had no such opportunity as was given to him before terminating their services. [801 E F] (iv) The principle that a workman should be given an adequate opportunity of explaining his conduct and giving any evidence in support thereof is not applicable to the present proceedings. [981 G H] (v) The principles laid down by this Court in the case of National Industrial Tribunal, Bombay vs K. M. Desai, ; , applied.

The appellant, a resident of Calcutta, was granted a lease of the land to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The lease deed provided that the lessee shall not assign or transfer any right in the site or any part thereof without the previous consent of the Government. The appellant applied for a lease and obtained an order from the Government of West Bengal, but the same was refused on the ground that it had been granted by the Government under section 3(1) of the . The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court in a writ petition which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the decision to lease the Begumbari land to Taj Group was taken on February 12, 1981; (ii) the Government had no power to grant four acres of Begumbar land to any person other than the Taj group of Hotels; and (iii) the order of the State Government was not in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision to grant 4 acres of the Begum land to a Taj Group is taken on March 12,1981. It is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government in taking a particular action, that the Court would have to decide whether the action of the Govern ment was reasonable and in public interest. [260F] 2. The purpose of the grant of four acres is to start with the construction industry and to provide for the establishment of industries within the State. It has been provided by the Act that the Government shall take steps to establish industries within its jurisdiction, and if so required, the Government may issue a notification in the Official Gazette specifying the areas which would be included in the area for the purpose of this Act. [261F] 3. The object of the Act is to provide a machinery for the regulation of the development of the area and for the prevention of exploitation of land by the State or for any other purposes connected with the development thereof. It also provides that the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 shall apply to all proceedings under the Act. The Act has been enacted in order to protect the interests of the people of India. [262G H] 4. The Government was quite alive to the need for expanse of the zoo. The proposed hotel is a Garden Hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting several trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and burning ground for rubbish. [263A] 5. The State has made available to this court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of land to respondent No. 1. It was on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances that the State had made available all documents, in connection therewith, to the appellant. The matter was taken in appeal. [264B] 6. The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence and has committed an error in holding that the land which was undoubt edly Government land, to start a Five star hotel, was given to the Tolaram for construction of five Star Hotel in Calcutta. The land allotted to the hotel was, as it was not used for the main purpose of building a Fivec Star hotel. [265C] 7. The question whether the land is required for the public purpose or not has to be determined on the basis of the materials placed before the Court and the material on record. It cannot be said that the High court has committed any error in granting the lease of Begum. [267D] 8. The grant of 4 acres was made by the Toraram for the construc tion of a five star hotel in Calcutta, which according to the Government was a prime need to the city of Calcutta.

The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The assessee claimed that the sum of Rs.67,560/12/ was wrongly included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Income Tax Officer rejected this claim on the ground that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.1 lakh on 1.1.1957 and Rs.50,000 on 31.1 .1957. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs,67,561/12 was rightly included in its net wealth. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no valid gift of the said amount and that the High Court had erred in answering the question in favour of the Revenue. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that the view taken by the High Courts in New India citation is correct. On behalf of respondent assessee it was submitted that the decision of the Delhi High Court in New Indian feature Co. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi, was not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering question in the manner it did. [130C] 2. In the instant case, the assessee had made a valid gift and trust in respect of the amount gifted could not be held to have been validly made by debiting the assessee 's personal account in the books of the Hindu undivided family with Rs. 50,000 and crediting the same in the personal account of his son. [131D] 3. The question whether there was a valid gifts or trust in the hands of the donee and gift in such case will not be valid. [132E] 4. In view of the fact that the entries in the accounts of the family were made contemporane ously shown to be fictitious, it resulted in a valid transfer of the shares of the donees by debit ing the assessee"s personal Account in the names of the minor donees and the amount was available to that firm or the company or H.U.F. on the date of gift, then a valid Gift by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or family or a company which was not a banking company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid gifted. [133F G] 5. The fact that a sum of money was not received in cash or in any other form with a bank or with a banking Company and that amount is available to the firm for being kept in the account of the father does not constitute a valid sale. [134G H] 6. In order to decide whether there is a valid receipt or trust, it is necessary to consider the nature of the gift as well as the source from which it was made. The test is whether the donor has received the money and the property is properly gifted or not. If the donor had received the amount in cash, he would have been able to get it back with the money. [135A B] 7. In a case where the assessee has a credit balance with firm or with family or with any banking company and that sum is available for being invested in the business of the firm which is not a bank, the proper gift by book entry may be possible But where a large amount was received by the donor and the money was available with him, the same would have to be returned. [136C D] 8. In such cases, the question whether the assessee received any sum in cash on 1st January 1957 or on 31st January,1957, does not arise. [137E] 9.

The appellant was a member of the Orissa High Court and was posted as Superintendent and legal remembrance. The High Court held that Shri B.K. Patro, district and sessions judges were not competent to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal person in charge of administrative posts as District Judges. The State Government issued an order dated October 10, 1966 directing the Chief Secretary to the Government of Orissa to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts to the cadre of district judges or as addl district judges as the case may be after they had held those posts for three years or more. On November 10, 1967 the High Court directed that the appellant should be posted as superintendent and Legal remembrancer in March 1962. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of the High. Court on the ground that he was not competent under article 233 to act on the basis of the order dated November 10 1966. The petition was dismissed by the High 'Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the order passed by the State Government holding that those officers had no authority to hold the posts in question is unsustainable; and (2) the High Courts were not empowered to issue a writ under article 226 of the Constitution as the power to appoint a district judge was vested in the State. HELD: (i) The High Courts are not competent in posting Shri BK. Sen, District and Sessions Judge, Ganjam, as superintendent or legal rem embassy. [626 D] (ii) The order of transfer passed by High Court is not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of it. It was beyond the powers of the Governor and fell to be made by the same Court as the law Secretary to Government of the State in charge.

The appellants, who were the sons of the vendor and vendors, filed a suit for pre emption against the respondent on the ground that they had purchased under tenan cy of the sale deed dated 10.12.1954 executed by their father in favour of the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and that there were no infringement or infringement of article 19(i)(f). On appeal, the High Court held that there had been no infringement and that the appellants had failed to prove their case. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers, he as a co shar holder could claim pre empt of the right of pre emment conferred on him by that provision. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the Act is to provide for the better regulation of sale and purchase of agricultural land in the State. Section 15(1) (a) provides that where a sale is of a share out of joint land or property, and is not made by all co sharists jointly, only the other co sharen ters and the tenants can exercise the right to pre empators. [127F G] 1.2 The object is to confer the right on specified family members of the vendors of the land or properties sold or a part thereof. It is not possible to lay down any general rule that the legislature intended to confer such a right on certain persons as co sharants. [128B C] 1:3. In the instant case, the suit lands belonged to several co sharators and had been purchased by all of them. The appellants were not in possession of the co co shar er or vendors of other co co co share.

The father of the appellant, who was a minor, executed a will in respect of certain properties in favour of his two sons and the same was registered on 21.8.1987. The said deed provided that the petitioner would pay Rs. 1 lakh to each of his three sons in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. On 21.9.1987, the father and his two brothers executed a compromise whereby they agreed to pay Rs 1 lakh each to each one of them in lieu thereof. The petitioner 's mother died on 22.8 .1987. In view of the said compromise, the petitioner filed an application for execution of the decree. On 20.9 .1987, when the matter was listed before the Court for recording of the compromise, Sudarshan Gupta, second respondent, maintained that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The Court passed a decree on 21st August 1987 in terms of the consent terms. On 22nd September 1987, the first respondent filed an execution petition for realisation of the amount due from the petitioner. The executing court passed an order directing the petitioner to pay the balance of Rs.77,124 being the amount paid by him before the registering authority. The first respondent challenged the said order in a suit for possession and injunction. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the court to record the same and no option lay before the court. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the sale deeds were subsequent to 21. 8 1987 and therefore the sale deed was not valid and binding on the alienees. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have to find out whether there was any compromise between the parties or not. If it is found that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence, then the court can act otherwise. [541C] 1.2 In the instant case, the alienee had accepted the fact that the parties have signed the compromise petition which contains terms which they had accepted and all parties have accepted the document of compromise to be genuine. The sale deeds are subsequent to the said agreement. The court has also directed that the amount of Rs 77,124 be deposited within the same period in the Trial Court and the alienors of different sale deeds would be entitled to withdraw the amounts on the basis of the record made by the Sub Registrar on each of the sale transactions. [542D E] 1:3. The question as to recording of compromise was not raised before the High Court. It is a matter of appreciation of evidence and it cannot be said that the court has acted perversely or otherwise improperly in passing the decree or that the transaction is vitiated by any error apparent on the face of record. [543E] 1 :4. The principle laid down in the aforesaid decision is applicable to the facts of this case. [544F] 1 Whether there was an agreement for sale subsequent to compromise for a sum of Rs 1,00,000 or not is a question of fact which has to be decided on the evidence and the parties are free to lead further evidence. The parties have been given liberty to adduce additional evidence in support of their respective contentions before the trial court.

The appellant company was entitled to sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sick leave. The workmen were not entitled to the sickness benefit under the Act. The Tribunal held that the benefits admissible under the provisions of the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and set aside the award in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the benefit of sick leaves should be granted only in the cases of sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner and not otherwise. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has made an award for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958 subject to the condition that the concession would cease to apply when the benefits of the Acts became available to the workmen. [84E] (2) The Act does not provide for any leave to the workman on the ground of sickness. It is only a rule of practice that the Tribunal should not, in any case, have given the benefit thereof. [85F G] (3) The expression "any other benefit" occurring in section 49 of the , has been used in contradistinction to the word "excluded". The expression 'in the case ' means 'in a case where the workman is entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act, he shall not be entitled to receive any similar benefit admissible under any other enactment. [86G H] (4) The object of the legislation is to provide for certain benefits to workmen on the grounds of sickness and maternity. It does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on half pay and Dearness allowance in the garb of sick or sick leave.[86G] (5) The word "in the absence of a contract" has been defined to mean "in any case where an industrial dispute is pending before a Tribunal. [87H; 88A] (6) The Industrial Tribunals have not given any reason for allowing the benefit to the appellant 's workmen for the initial waiting period of two days except in cases of continuous illness following at the interval of more than fifteen days, and even that amount is not admissible for the second two days also.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Drug Offenders and Dangerous Activities Act, 1958. The grounds furnished to him were that he had been indulging in various activities prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and that he was carrying on espionage activities which were prejudicial to public order. He challenged his detention by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that (1) the detaining authority had not given him the opportunity of making a representation against the order, (2) the grounds supplied to him did not disclose any particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by him and (3) the impugned order was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the grounds furnished were vague or not in the sense that they were vague. The ground supplied was not vague or did not indicate the source from which it could be inferred. The power of detention can be exercised only when there is a clear and cogent material to show that the person concerned has been acting in a manner prejudicial to maintenance of law and order. In the present case, the grounds were not vague nor did they contain any particulars as to how the petitioner was indulging in the activities prejudicial or subversive of public tranquility. The fact that the detaining authorities had not mentioned the names of the persons who were alleged to be involved in the incident, could not make out a case for interference under article 22(6) of tile Constitution. The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 21 of the Constitu tion and the failure to mention these matters in the particular paragraph of the affidavit filed by the detenue would vitiate his detention.

The respondent was a member of the General Court Martial. He was dismissed from service by an order dated September 9, 1959. The Central Government directed removal from service under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. On April 9, 1960, the Chief of the Military Staff passed an order removing him from service. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal on the ground that r.14 was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r 14 was ultra rites as it was not ultra vires. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 14 is a self contained code and does not offend article 14 of Constitution. [449 B] (ii) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" in r. 15 are wide enough to include within its ambit the power to remove an officer from the service. Rule 14 was therefore ultra vires as it contravened articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [445 C D] (iii) The word "subject" in section 19 makes it clear that there should be rules, and subject to the provision of the Act and such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the Service any person subject to this Act. [453 E] (iv) Rule 15 is a general rule which deals with punishment for misconduct against an officer whose further retention in service is not considered desirable. The words 'subject to this provision ' occurring in section 191 make it clear of the intention of the legislature that there must be rules and subject thereto, the central Government has been given the power under r, 14 to dismiss or removal from the serv ice any person. [454 G] (v) Rule 16 is a special rule which provides for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45. The two sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive. They deal with the procedure for imposing penalties. Rule 15 deals with dismissal or removal of an officer who has been dismissed from the services. Rule 16(1) does not contain any specific provision for punishment.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing tea. The Government of Bombay issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, exempting the factory from octroi duty for consumption, use or sale. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the notification was invalid because it did not specify the rate at which it was to be levied and that the Government had no power under section 23(1)(a) of Bombay District Municipalities Act, 1922, to levy octroi duty on tea imported into the Panchayat limits for consumption use or sold. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The notification issued by the Government did not contain any provision requiring the Panchayat to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules. [218 E] The word "may" in section 23 (1)(b) of that Act, does not mean that the Panchayat should have the power to impose octroi duty. It is only when a panchayat finally decides to levy any tax or fee that it can impose the tax or fees. [282 F G] The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. [220 B C] The appellant did not say whether the tea was crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. The notification dated January 14, 1964, relates back and therefore the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963, was regularised. [221 F G].

The appellant No. 1 was employed in the respondent company as a driver and proceedings were taken on a complaint by the Conciliation Officer under section 33 read with section 31(1) of the , against the appellants. The conciliation proceedings commenced at the instance of the appellant No 1 and the conciliation proceedings were held on December 13, 1951, but the conciliation proceeding was not concluded within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation Proceedings or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The respondent filed a complaint before the Conciliation officer under section 31 read with sections 33 and 33(1). The appellants contended that as the conciliation had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under section 30(1), read with s.33(1); Held, that the conciliation was not completed within 14th day of the date fixed by Government under section 12(6) of Act and the proceedings were not concluded on December 31, 1951. The provisions of the Act do not apply to the proceedings before the conciliation officer as they are not commenced after January 17. 1952, but when that report is received by the State Government it cannot be said that the proceedings did not commence until January 17 and terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of that Act. The words " pending conciliation proceedings" in section 12 (6) refer to a dispute pending before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal under section 10 during the pendency of conciliation proceedings.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was a member of an unlawful assembly and was likely to be enlarged on bail. The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing between two rival groups, and that the petitioner had disturbed the normal tempo of life in Katras and Jogta Police Station. The detaining authority after considering all the relevant factors, passed the order of detention. The petitioner challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order was made on one incident relating to exchange of fire between two groups and that there were no materials for passing the order, and therefore the detention was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive detention passed by the respondent no.1 is set aside. [910C] 2. In a case where the actual order of release was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there Was such a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. [099D] 3. The detention order was set aside on the sole ground that the detenu 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. It is not stated that this fact or the questions that the detaining authoritY had given any opportunity to the detenu to explain his position. If that is the position, then however, it is inconceivable that the antecedents of a person might have been without consideration of all the aforesaid relevant factors. [109E F] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Burdwan & Anr., ; , referred to.

The respondent firm, manufacturers of gold and silver, was manufacturing gold. The firm had a stock in the name of its partners. In the year 1965, the firm purchased gold from the firm. The stock in trade was found to be more than Rs. 1 lac. The Income Tax Officer assessed the firm as a dealer under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment and held that the firm had failed to prove its case against it. In further revision, the High Court set aside the order holding that the assessee was not entitled to any relief on the ground of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon him thereunder could be exercised by the Administrator but that is not decisive of the matter. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts ' decision in unamended sec. 28 of 1968 has resulted from excessive delegation and that the provisions of section 28 are violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the power to grant or renew a license to a dealer is not absolute but conditional upon the Administrator having regard to the policy and purpose of the Act, and by reference thereto, the power is conferred on him. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The objective of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide in the economic and financial interests of the community", for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold. [955C] 1.2 In the absence of any specific provision in the Act or the scheme of the enactment providing sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section, it is not obligatory upon him to exercise his discretion in the manner he has done. The purpose and object of the statute is to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Acts in making his orders. [936D] 1:3. In order to be a valid law, it must be made by the legislature with the object of promoting the interest of the general public. It does not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealers but he is prevented only from carrying out his obligations under that Act in making such orders. The object and purpose underlying the enactment and the scheme are to ensure speedy disposal of cases by the authorities concerned. [951E F] 1 :4. In view of the fact that the legislature has not provided for any criteria or guidelines for guiding the discretion of the Administrator, it cannot be struck down on the grounds of excessive delegations of legislative powers. [953F G] 1 5. The objective is to provide in economic and industrial interests of a class of persons who are engaged in business as dealers but they are prevented only by the authority of law from carrying them out their duties in accordance with the Act. [948A B] 1 6.

The appellants were the owners of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk. The suit was filed by the respondents against four respondents claiming that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit and the first appellate Court found that the title of the alienees in regard to 'dharmadlayam properties had not been acquired by adverse possession before the suit was instituted, but it held that the appellants had acquired title by adverse posses sion prior to 1 1 1929. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decisions of the courts below and held that they had not acquired title to the properties in question. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contention that the suit filed by respondents 1 to 3 was barred by limitation is without substance. It is open to doubt whether the decision could lead to the inference that if a part of the property is transferred by the manager of a religious endowment on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowment, the transfer is void ab initio, with the result that the possession and enjoyment of the transferee is adverse to the community from the date of the transfer. [866 D F] (ii) The question as to whether a transfer effected by the Manager of a temple in regard tO properties belonging to the temple falls outside the purview of article 134 B is not a mixed question of fact and law, and the High Courts were right in reversing the decisions. [886 E G] (iii) The High Court was in error in reversing those decisions by holding that the property belonged to the deity.

The appellant firm was carrying on the business of cinema business in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu was granted by the District Magistrate in favour of the firm. The firm applied to the District Magis trate for a renewal of the licence. The District Magistrate rejected the request on the ground that the licence had been granted to the firm and that it had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the High Court. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Government against the order of the District magistrate. The State Government dismissed the appeal holding that the renewal of a licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, the licensee, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsar Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977 which was confirmed in appeal by the State Govt. and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ appeal filed by the firm against the orders of the Sub Divisional Magistrate. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to suspend a licence which could be made only in the names of the original licensees, namely the licensee and there was no mention at all of the partners of the Firm or its partners. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Sub Divnt Magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [578F] 2. The licensing authority has no power to suspend the licence which can be made under section 6 F of the Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authori ty had no jurisdiction to suspend it. [579A B] 3. The only reason stated by the high Court for quashing the District Commissioner 's order is that the District Magistrates had no authority under the . Act or Rules to make such an order. [580C D] 4. The power to suspended a licence is conferred only by section 6F of the , as one implied in the wider power of revoking and unless there is any provision in the Act, the rules framed thereunder cannot be deemed to have been repealed. [581D] 5. The mere fact that the licensee has been declared an insolvent or a person holding an office under him does not by itself make him a party to the proceedings for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the license and answerable to the licensing authorities for all commissions and omissions in the cinema premises. [583E F] 6.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain properties in Pakistan, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the purchase of certain mills and factory in question. The terms of the agreement were that the mills would be leased to them for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants under section 12 of the Act, terminating the lease. The appellants challenged the validity of the notice by filing a petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian and set aside the order of termination. On appeal by certificate, Held, that section 10 Of the Act did not apply to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself. The provisions of section 10 of the Bombay Act were applicable only to leases issued by the evacuees and not to leases executed by them. The words "any lease" in section 12 meant a transfer of property made for consideration and not for any other purpose. The word "transfer" in the context means a transfer for consideration, and therefore, it could not be said that the Custodian had no power under section 10 to cancel the lease granted by himself. It was not correct to say that the words "by the evacuee" in s.12 were intended to include a transfer made for valuable consideration. The effect of the sale was that the property was transferred to the evacuee, and the property could be sold only if it was found that there was no valid contract between the parties. The Custodian had the power under s.10 to cancel a lease granted in favour of the appellants, but he did not do so. The right of the appellant to cancel an agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them was not affected by section 10. The rights of the parties were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and that nothing in the Act should be taken as a pronouncement on those rights.

The appellant was a minor son of the respondent. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 5th May, 1976 determined the ceiling area but an appeal by Raghubir Singh to the Revenue Appellate Authority was dismissed on March 6, 1973 and the Board of Revenue set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer on March 7, 1973. The appellant filed a revision application before the Board which allowed the same and remanded the case to the Sub Divi sion Officer Hanumangadha, who by his orders dated 5.5.1976 directed that the ceiling should be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to new law i954. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by the Single Judge on 19th July, 1979. The Board of revenue set aside its order dated 6th August, 1977 and remanded it for fresh determination of the ceiling. The sub Divisional Officer held that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order passed by the Sub divisional Officer and dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant. The writ petition filed by respondent before the High court was allowed and the order dated 19th June, 1976 was set aside. The State Government preferred an appeal to the Board against the order dismissing the writ petition of the sub divisional officer. The Division Bench of the High COurt dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no appeal having been filed by State from the order the Sub Division Officer dated 5 5 1976 became final and the respondent in his favour was set at liberty to file a revision petition under section 230 of the Act of 1956 before the Revenue Appel late Authority. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that it is not correct to say that Section 9 is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Board over subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. [726C] 2.1 Section 221 of the Government of India Act, 1915 is similar to section 107 of the Govern ment of India. The Boards of Revenue have general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts.

The first respondent, the Chief Controller of Sales Tax, was appointed as an Assistant Commissioner of Sales tax in the State of Orissa. The first respondent was appointed by the Central Government as a Sales Tax Officer on ad hoc basis for a period of two years. He was later promoted as Additional Sales Tax officer. In the year 1973 he was served with a notice under section 9(2) of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be called upon to pay the tax due from him. The second respondent challenged the said notice by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The High Court held that the first respondent had no locus standi to file the writ petition and quashed the order of the Central Govern ment on the ground that the law reports published by it were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the State Government on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable. The appellant filed a Special Leave Petition before this Court against the said judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports which are being published by the Ist respondent are reports of recent decisions of the Supreme Court and of the high Courts in India which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [778C] 1.2 In the instant case, the first Respondent has not been able to agree with the second respondent that the Law reports do not carry any news and that the public was not interested in them. The law report published by a Ist respondent contains information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme court or in the high courts which are Public bodies and those are matters of public importance. [779D] 1:3. In view of the fact that the expression 'newspaper ' as defined under the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news ', it is difficult to agree that the publication of the recent judgments itself is sufficient to make a law report a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute the one which advances the object of the legislation and is in favour of the employee for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [780E F] 1 :4.
